lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Here's a good test for a data platform. When someone says we cannot expose that table, does the tool help or get in the way?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: I'd guess most of them get in the way.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: That's what Antoine wanted to hear about at Snowflake Data-for-Breakfast, a morning conference with an Infostrux keynote. He went for how teams actually run Snowflake, not for swag. He had enough SQL to be dangerous, he says, but not enough production stories.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: And what was the big framing?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: The opening deck pitched Snowflake as governed sharing first, raw speed second. That order matters when your fear is exposing the wrong data, not needing another cluster.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: A healthcare customer ran secure operations across three continents, sharing partner data without losing availability. The lessons were that compliance can't be an afterthought when partners query live, and clinical operations can't live on overnight batch alone.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: A tax-sector team landed very large datasets and explored them without knowing every question upfront. One consolidation layer sped up troubleshooting and made lineage easier to explain to auditors. And analysts stopped emailing CSV attachments.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Ha. And I keep hearing clean rooms.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: That was the third one. Two companies compare overlapping datasets for due diligence without dumping everything into one bucket. Antoine calls it a product story, not just a compliance checkbox.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: His notes flag cost without query discipline, and warehouses left running after an exploratory spike.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So what did he take home?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Clearer vocabulary for customer conversations, even when he isn't on Snowflake day to day. The full write-up has his comparison table.
